$comment: Self-hosted applications that send a small amount of mail to their own operator. Every field name and value here was read off the vendor's own documentation on the date in `updated` - none of it is recalled. `caveat` is not optional: an entry without an honest limit is an advert.

entries.name: Immich
entries.what: a self-hosted photo and video library, usually run for a household or a small group
sends: a notification when a new user is created
a notification to a user added to a shared album
a notification when new assets are added to a shared album
entries.why_it_fits: Immich mails people you already know, a handful of times a month. It is not sending receipts to strangers, so the sending domain carries no trust that matters here.
entries.where: Administration -> Settings -> Notification settings, in the web interface. The fields are the ordinary SMTP ones and are edited in the browser rather than in a file.
entries.caveat: Immich's own documentation does not name the individual SMTP fields, so this page does not pretend to quote them. Match the values below to the labelled boxes on that screen.

entries.name: Vaultwarden
entries.what: a self-hosted server for the Bitwarden clients, run by one person for a family, a team or themselves
sends: invitations to new users, valid for five days
verification, password-hint and two-factor mail, when those features are on
entries.why_it_fits: An invitation is sent once per person, ever. A password vault that stops sending invitations has no other way to add anybody, and the volume never approaches a daily cap.
entries.where: Environment variables, usually in the `docker-compose.yml` or `.env` beside it.
entries.caveat: `SMTP_FROM` has to be the generated address, not your own domain. Vaultwarden will start with a mismatched one and the mail will be refused or filed as spam, which looks like Vaultwarden failing.

entries.name: Gitea
entries.what: a self-hosted Git service, typically a few users on one machine
sends: notifications on issues and pull requests people are watching
entries.why_it_fits: A private instance with a handful of accounts sends a trickle. Registration and resets are what actually matter: without them a locked-out user stays locked out.
entries.caveat: This is the entry on this page most likely to outgrow the 200-a-day cap. Issue and pull-request notifications multiply by the number of watchers, so a busy instance with a dozen active people can pass it without anybody noticing until mail stops.

entries.name: Authelia
entries.what: an authentication and two-factor portal sitting in front of everything else somebody self-hosts
sends: identity-verification mail when a user registers a second factor
entries.why_it_fits: Authelia mails a person once, at the moment they set up or recover access. The volume is tiny and the stakes are not: if this mail cannot leave, nobody can enrol a second factor or recover an account.
entries.caveat: Authelia's `address` is a URI with a scheme, not a bare hostname. `submission://` means STARTTLS on 587 and `submissions://` means implicit TLS on 465 - one letter apart, and getting it wrong produces a connection error rather than an authentication one, which sends people looking in the wrong place.

entries.name: Paperless-ngx
entries.what: a self-hosted document archive that scans, indexes and stores paperwork for a household or a small office
sends: password resets and account mail for the people who use it
notifications about documents shared by link
entries.why_it_fits: Paperless mostly reads mail rather than sending it - its headline feature is pulling documents out of a mailbox. The outgoing side is small and internal: resets and share notices, to people who already have an account on your server.
entries.where: Environment variables, usually in `docker-compose.env` beside the compose file.
entries.caveat: The defaults are `localhost` on port 25 with `PAPERLESS_EMAIL_USE_TLS` set to false. All six values have to be set: leaving TLS off sends the password in the clear and the relay refuses it, which surfaces as a connection error rather than an authentication one and sends people looking at the wrong thing. `PAPERLESS_EMAIL_FROM` falls back to `PAPERLESS_EMAIL_HOST_USER`, so setting the user correctly fixes both - but set it anyway rather than relying on a default that may change.

entries.name: changedetection.io
entries.what: a self-hosted tool that watches a webpage or a JSON API and alerts when it changes
sends: a notification when a watched page changes, to whoever set up the watch
entries.why_it_fits: One alert per change, to the person who configured the watch. Nobody outside that person ever sees the sender address, so the generated one costs nothing here.
entries.where: Settings -> Notifications, as an Apprise URL - the app itself does not have SMTP fields; it hands the string straight to the Apprise library, so the syntax is Apprise's, not changedetection's.
entries.caveat: The part after @ in an Apprise mailto URL is read as the mail server unless smtp= overrides it - our sender address and our relay host are two different names (msgwing.com vs mx.msgwing.com), so leaving out smtp= sends it to the wrong place with no error until the alert never arrives. mailtos:// defaults to port 587 with TLS; do not add a port unless you need 465.

entries.name: n8n
entries.what: a self-hosted workflow automation platform - the free alternative to Zapier, used to wire alerts and notifications between other self-hosted tools
sends: whatever a workflow is built to send - failure alerts, status digests, form-submission notices - through its Send Email node, to whoever the workflow author configured
entries.why_it_fits: The volume is whatever the workflows generate, decided by the person who built them, and n8n itself imposes no floor. A homelab running a handful of alert workflows never approaches 200 a day; a business running high-volume campaigns through n8n is the wrong audience for this regardless of the limit.
entries.where: Credentials -> New -> Send Email, in the web UI.
entries.caveat: n8n exposes SSL/TLS as one toggle rather than a STARTTLS-vs-implicit-TLS choice. Leave SSL/TLS on and Disable STARTTLS off for port 587 - the two settings sound like opposites and are not: the second only matters when the first is off, and toggling both off at once sends the password unencrypted.

entries.name: Netdata
entries.what: a self-hosted, real-time monitoring agent for a server or a fleet of them
sends: health alerts when a monitored metric crosses a threshold - disk full, CPU pinned, a service down
entries.why_it_fits: An alert fires only when something is actually wrong, to the person running the server. Volume is naturally low unless something is badly broken, and nobody outside that person sees the sender address.
entries.where: Netdata itself has no SMTP fields - health_alarm_notify.conf only turns email on and sets the sender/recipient. The actual relay is delegated to the sendmail command on the host, or - the common case in Docker - to msmtp, configured in msmtprc.
entries.caveat: These are msmtp directives, not Netdata's own configuration - Netdata calls whatever sendmail-compatible binary is on the PATH and has no visibility into whether it works. A misconfigured msmtprc fails silently from Netdata's side: the alert fires, Netdata believes it sent, and nothing arrives. Test with the command "echo test | msmtp your@address" before trusting an alert to reach anyone.

entries.name: Jellyfin
entries.what: a self-hosted media server for films, television and music, usually run for one household
sends: a message when an item is added to the library, to whoever runs the server
authentication failures, successful logins and a user being locked out
scheduled-task completions, plugin installs and pending-restart notices
entries.why_it_fits: Jellyfin's notifications go to whoever runs the server, not to the people watching, and the SMTP destination takes exactly one Receiver Address - so there is no audience deciding whether to trust the sender. Whether it stays under 200 a day is a choice you make when you tick the notification types rather than a property of Jellyfin: Item Added on a library that imports a season at a time, or Playback Progress on any library at all, will pass the cap in an afternoon.
entries.where: Jellyfin does not send email itself. Its own documentation says notifications appear on the dashboard and that anything else goes [through the Webhook plugin](https://jellyfin.org/docs/general/server/notifications/) - so mail exists only there. Install it from Dashboard -> Plugins -> Catalog, where it is filed under **Administration** rather than under notifications, restart the server, then open Dashboard -> Plugins -> Webhook and use Add SMTP Destination. These are the labels on that form.
fields: your own inbox, where you want the alerts
entries.caveat: 465 is not a typo and 587 will not work here. Use SSL is not a STARTTLS toggle: the plugin passes SslOnConnect when it is ticked and no encryption whatsoever when it is not, and it offers no third option - so 587 either meets a client expecting implicit TLS or sends your password in the clear for the relay to refuse. Both mistakes are invisible from Jellyfin. Every send failure is caught and written as a single warning line to the server log, so the notification looks delivered and nothing arrives. Turn on debug logging for Jellyfin.Plugin.Webhook in logging.json before you trust an alert to reach you. Jellyfin's prose documentation never names an SMTP field, so the labels above are read off the configuration form the plugin itself ships, linked below - not quoted from a manual page that does not exist.
